patient.chief_complaint: Woke up with slurred speech and clumsiness of the right hand
patient.history_present_illness: Mr. Michael Patterson is a 73-year-old right-handed Caucasian man with a history of poorly controlled hypertension, type 2 diabetes, hyperlipidemia, obstructive sleep apnea, and chronic kidney disease who presents to the emergency department after waking at approximately 06:45 this morning with new-onset slurred speech and difficulty using his right hand. He reports going to bed at approximately 23:00 the previous evening feeling entirely at his baseline. He woke once around 03:00 to use the bathroom and does not recall any difficulty at that time, though he acknowledges he was groggy and did not pay close attention to his coordination or speech. When his alarm went off at 06:45, he noticed his speech sounded thick and he had trouble gripping his phone. He also felt mildly unsteady when walking to the bathroom. He initially attributed these symptoms to having slept in an awkward position and waited approximately 45 minutes to see if they would resolve. When the symptoms persisted, his daughter called him at 07:30 during her morning routine, noticed his slurred speech over the phone, and urged him to call 911. EMS arrived at 07:52 and identified right facial droop and mild right arm weakness. A prehospital stroke alert was activated with a Cincinnati Prehospital Stroke Scale score of 2. His fingerstick glucose in the field was 204 mg/dL. He arrived at the ED at 08:14. On initial assessment, the patient reports a mild headache over the left temporal region but denies any visual changes, nausea, vomiting, chest pain, or seizure-like activity. He cannot say for certain whether the symptoms were present when he woke at 03:00, making the last known well time approximately 23:00 the previous evening, roughly 9 hours prior to ED arrival. This exceeds the standard 4.5-hour window for IV thrombolysis and complicates acute management decisions. He has no history of prior stroke or TIA. He ran out of his amlodipine approximately one week ago and has not refilled it.

results.title: MRI-Guided Thrombolysis for Stroke with Unknown Time of Onset (WAKE-UP Trial)
results.authors: Thomalla G, Simonsen CZ, et al.
results.key_finding: IV alteplase improved functional outcome in wake-up stroke patients selected by DWI-FLAIR mismatch (DWI positive, FLAIR negative), indicating onset within ~4.5 hours.

results.title: Extending thrombolysis to 4.5-9 hours using perfusion imaging (EXTEND Trial)
results.authors: Ma H, Campbell BCV, et al.
results.key_finding: IV alteplase between 4.5-9h from onset or in wake-up stroke benefited patients with penumbral mismatch on CT or MRI perfusion imaging.

results.title: 2019 AHA/ASA Guideline Update for Early Management of Acute Ischemic Stroke
results.authors: Powers WJ, Rabinstein AA, et al.
results.key_finding: In wake-up stroke, if DWI-FLAIR mismatch is present, IV alteplase may be considered. If FLAIR is already positive, this suggests onset >4.5 hours and standard thrombolysis criteria may not be met.

output.summary: For wake-up strokes with unknown onset time, the WAKE-UP trial demonstrated that DWI-FLAIR mismatch on MRI can identify patients who may benefit from IV thrombolysis. A DWI-positive/FLAIR-negative mismatch suggests onset within approximately 4.5 hours. When both DWI and FLAIR are positive, the stroke likely occurred more than 4.5 hours ago, and standard IV thrombolysis is generally not recommended. The EXTEND trial showed that CT or MRI perfusion-based selection can extend the treatment window to 9 hours in patients with a significant penumbral mismatch.

contraindicated_actions: Do not administer IV tPA before non-contrast CT excludes intracranial hemorrhage
Do not give IV tPA if INR >1.7, platelet count <100,000, recent major surgery, or other guideline-listed contraindications
Do not aggressively lower blood pressure below 140/90 mmHg in the acute phase outside the tPA window — risks worsening penumbral perfusion
Do not delay non-contrast CT for additional imaging or labs in a stroke alert presentation
Do not start full-dose anticoagulation in the acute phase of a large infarct without considering hemorrhagic transformation risk
Do not treat as purely large-artery atherosclerotic without confirmatory cardiac monitoring
Avoid order_ct_scan with contrast=True, angiography=True: Iodinated contrast carries nephrotoxicity risk in CKD stage 3a; mitigate or substitute MR angiography when feasible
key_reasoning_points: Acute ischemic stroke is a clinical syndrome plus neuroimaging diagnosis; CT first excludes hemorrhage and unmasks the tPA decision
Time of last known well governs IV thrombolysis eligibility (≤4.5h standard; selected up to 9h with imaging mismatch per WAKE-UP/EXTEND)
Large vessel occlusion on CTA opens the mechanical thrombectomy pathway up to 24h per DAWN/DEFUSE-3 selection criteria
TOAST classification by mechanism (large-artery, cardioembolic, small-vessel, other, undetermined) drives secondary prevention strategy
Normal sinus rhythm on initial ECG does NOT exclude paroxysmal AF — extended cardiac monitoring is required, especially in cryptogenic stroke
Cortical MCA-superior-division infarcts are typically embolic; cardiac source workup is essential
Left atrial enlargement increases pretest probability of paroxysmal AF and warrants prolonged monitoring
Off-pathway modality for order_advanced_imaging (modality=amyloid_PET): Amyloid PET has no role in acute ischemic stroke evaluation and incurs substantial cost without altering management
Off-pathway modality for order_advanced_imaging (modality=DaTscan): Dopamine transporter SPECT is indicated for parkinsonian syndromes, not vascular stroke workup
Off-pathway modality for order_advanced_imaging (modality=FDG_PET): FDG-PET (neurodegenerative/oncologic indications) has no role in routine ischemic stroke workup

metadata.difficulty_description: Moderate - wake-up stroke with subtle right-sided neglect and mild dysarthria, no AF on initial ECG but left atrial enlargement as a clue, chronic white matter disease complicating MRI interpretation
clinical_pearls: The WAKE-UP trial established DWI-FLAIR mismatch as a tissue clock for wake-up strokes: DWI+/FLAIR- suggests onset within 4.5 hours and eligibility for thrombolysis; DWI+/FLAIR+ suggests onset beyond 4.5 hours
Up to 25% of cryptogenic strokes in patients over 55 are attributed to paroxysmal AF detected on prolonged monitoring; a single ECG is insufficient to exclude this diagnosis
Left atrial enlargement on ECG or echocardiography is a strong predictor of underlying paroxysmal atrial fibrillation and should lower the threshold for prolonged cardiac monitoring
Hemineglect with a dominant (left) hemisphere lesion is less common and typically more subtle than with non-dominant (right) hemisphere strokes, making it easier to miss on routine examination
metadata.difficulty_rationale: Wake-up MCA stroke, cardioembolic from paroxysmal AF; tissue-clock decision and mechanism assignment require multimodal synthesis.
